newsitem.title: INDIA: India to join hands with neighbours on electricity.
newsitem.headline: India to join hands with neighbours on electricity.

text.p: Power-starved India will boost its efforts with its neighbours to improve cross-border flows of electricity to bolster regional economic growth, Power Minister Y.K. Alagh said on Friday.
"India has a firm commitment to inter-regional flows within South Asia and a wider region," Alagh told a business seminar.
"With Bangladesh, we already had a discussion under the aegis of the Asian Development Bank," he said.
Alagh said India's Powergrid Corp would soon meet its Bangladeshi counterpart to discuss transmissions.
"With Pakistan, contacts have been made," he said. India is currently negotiating the import of 3,000 megawatts of power from Pakistan.

"These are aspects of the Gujral doctrine," Alagh said, referring to Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's philosophy that India should give unilateral concessions to its smaller neighbours. These include arch-rival Pakistan, with which India has fought three wars since independence from Britain in 1947.
"Kyrgyzstan wants to ship hydel power to us," Alagh said, adding that transportation links with Central Asian nations had been improved in recent years.
Alagh told a committee of lawmakers last week that the government would announce a new power policy after the monsoon session of parliament, which is scheduled to start in the third week of July.
"We do need now a quantitative configuration of the shape of things to come," Alagh told Reuters after the seminar.
"Apart from meeting short-run problems there is the question of making India's energy system work more optimally," he said.
Electricity generation grew by just 3.8 percent in 1996/97 (April-March), compared with 8.1 percent in 1995/96, the government said in a statement released on Friday.
During the Eighth Plan (1992-97), India could create fresh capacity for only 17,700 megawatts against a targeted 30,538 megawatts. The shortfall is mainly attributed to flagging investment.
Planning Commission officials say about 40,000 megawatts of additional power is expected to be generated in the Ninth Five-Year Plan against an official estimate of 50,000 megawatts.
Industry officials said state electricity boards (SEBs), pushed to financial bankruptcy by huge subsidies, were the weakest link in power sector reforms.
Many states are giving free power to farmers, leading to massive government subsidy payouts and affecting the performance of SEBs, they said.
"The question is one of working out modalities at the state level," Alagh said, adding that the new policy would address some of the problems faced by SEBs.
